To the BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

## NHANES — BMI and systolic blood pressure

Among NHANES participants aged 40–79, is body mass index (BMI) associated with systolic blood pressure?

I will use the `NHANES` dataset from the R package of the same name. It is a resampled version of the 2009–2010 and 2011–2012 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data collected by the U.S. National Center for Health Statistics. [NHANES R package documentation](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/NHANES/html/NHANES.html)

The study population includes NHANES participants aged 40–79 years. The unit of analysis is the individual participant.

The exposure is body mass index (BMI, kg/m²), treated as a continuous variable. The outcome is systolic blood pressure (BPSysAve, mmHg), also treated as a continuous variable.

Participants with missing BMI or systolic blood pressure will be excluded from the primary analysis. I will report how many participants are missing each variable and how many were excluded in total.

In the adjusted model, I will include age, recorded sex, race and ethnicity, smoking history, and survey cycle.

Among participants with both BMI and systolic blood pressure data, those missing any adjustment variable will be excluded from the adjusted analysis. I will report the number excluded at this step and the final sample size for the adjusted model.

I will create a scatterplot with BMI on the horizontal axis and systolic blood pressure on the vertical axis to visualize the relationship between the two variables. I will then fit a multiple linear regression model with systolic blood pressure as the outcome, BMI as the main predictor, and the covariates listed above to estimate the adjusted difference in mean systolic blood pressure (mmHg) associated with a 1 kg/m² higher BMI.

## CDC — Seasonality of waterborne disease outbreaks

Among U.S. waterborne disease outbreaks reported for 2009–2023, how did the distribution by month of the year differ across water exposure categories?

I will use the `waterborne` dataset included in the BST 260 project template. It is derived from the CDC’s National Outbreak Reporting System (NORS), which collects outbreak reports from state, local, and territorial health departments. [CDC NORS data documentation](https://www.cdc.gov/nors/data/)

The study population consists of U.S. waterborne disease outbreaks recorded in the CDC dataset for 2009–2023. The unit of analysis is an individual reported outbreak.

The exposure variable is the reported water exposure category (water_exposure), a categorical variable that includes exposures such as drinking water, treated recreational water, and untreated recreational water.

The outcome is the calendar month of the earliest reported illness onset in each outbreak (month), treated as a categorical variable with 12 levels from January through December.

For the main comparison, I will include outbreaks with a recorded onset month and a single, identified water exposure category. I will report the number of outbreaks excluded because of missing information, undetermined water exposure, or multiple recorded exposure categories.

In a secondary analysis, I will account for geographic region and outbreak year. Both the types of water exposure and the timing of outbreaks may vary by region. Including outbreak year will help account for changes over time in the types of outbreaks reported to CDC.

For each water exposure category, I will calculate the percentage of outbreaks that began in each calendar month. I will plot these percentages from January through December, using one line per exposure category to compare seasonal patterns.
